Alternate Name: Sri Hayagriva Jayanti/ Hayagriva Avatar Jayanti
Deity: Lord Hayagriva (Horse-headed incarnation of Lord Vishnu)
Historical Background: Celebrates the birth of Lord Hayagriva, the horse-headed incarnation of Lord Vishnu, who restored the stolen Vedas to Lord Brahma, symbolizing the victory of knowledge over ignorance.
Rituals: Worship of Lord Hayagriva, Vishnu Sahasranama and Hayagriva Stotram recitation, fasting, special puja, Vedic chanting, Upakarma observance by Brahmins.
Fair Activities: Temple worship, Vedic chanting, bhajans, religious discourses, prasadam distribution, community prayers, cultural programs.
Cultural Significance: Symbolizes the preservation of sacred knowledge and wisdom. Students and scholars worship Lord Hayagriva for intelligence, learning, and academic success.

Duration: 1 Day (Purnima Tithi: 12:38 PM on Aug 27 – 01:18 PM on Aug 28, 2026)
Historical Background: Sanskrit Diwas has been observed annually since 1969 to promote Sanskrit, regarded as the mother of many Indian languages and the language of the Vedas. It is celebrated on Shravana Purnima to preserve and encourage the study and use of Sanskrit.
Rituals: Sanskrit recitation, Vedic chanting, seminars, workshops, lectures, essay competitions, debates, cultural programs, and educational activities.
Fair Activities: Sanskrit competitions, exhibitions, seminars, workshops, educational programs, cultural performances, and Vedic recitations.
Cultural Significance: Promotes the preservation of Sanskrit, India's ancient literary and Vedic heritage, while encouraging linguistic, cultural, and scholarly development.

Alternate Name: Krishnashtami/Gokulashtami/ Ashtami Rohini/ Srikrishna Jayanti/Sree Jayanthi
Deity: Lord Krishna (8th incarnation of Lord Vishnu)
Duration: 1–2 Days (depending on Smarta and Vaishnava traditions; fasting may continue until the next day)
Historical Background: Krishna Janmashtami commemorates the birth of Lord Krishna, the eighth incarnation of Lord Vishnu, born in Mathura to destroy evil and restore Dharma. The festival celebrates his divine life, teachings, and role in the Mahabharata and Bhagavad Gita. Different traditions (Smarta and Vaishnava) may observe the festival on different dates based on Ashtami Tithi, Rohini Nakshatra, and Nishita Kaal.
Rituals: Day-long fasting, Sankalpa, midnight (Nishita Kaal) Krishna Puja, Shodashopachara Puja, Abhishekam of Bal Krishna, devotional singing (bhajans and kirtans), Bhagavad Gita reading, Jhulan (cradle ceremony), Dahi Handi celebrations (in many regions), and Parana after sunrise when Ashtami Tithi and Rohini Nakshatra end.
Fair Activities: Temple processions, Jhankis (tableaux), Dahi Handi competitions, Ras Leela performances, devotional music, cultural programs, community feasts, and midnight celebrations.
Cultural Significance: Symbolizes the victory of righteousness over evil, devotion (Bhakti), Dharma, compassion, and the divine teachings of Lord Krishna. It strengthens spiritual values and cultural unity among devotees.

Duration: 1 Day (Fast on 7 Sept 2026; Parana: 8 Sept 2026, 05:14 AM–07:46 AM; Dwadashi ends at 06:12 PM)
Historical Background: Aja Ekadashi is one of the 24 sacred Ekadashis dedicated to Lord Vishnu. According to the Brahma Vaivarta Purana, observing this fast grants liberation from sins and spiritual upliftment. It is associated with King Harishchandra, who regained his kingdom and family after observing this fast as advised by Sage Gautama.
Rituals: Nirjala or Phalahar fasting, Sankalpa, worship of Lord Vishnu, Vishnu Sahasranama recitation, reading Aja Ekadashi Vrat Katha, night vigil (Jagran), charity, and Parana after sunrise on Dwadashi.
Fair Activities: Temple worship, bhajans, kirtans, Vrat Katha recitation, devotional gatherings, charity (daan), and distribution of prasadam.
Cultural Significance: Emphasizes devotion, self-discipline, purification, and the removal of sins. It is believed to bestow prosperity, peace, and ultimately Moksha (liberation).

Hindu Month: Chaitra Krishna Paksha (North India – Purnimanta) / Phalguna Krishna Paksha (South India – Amanta)
Duration: 1 Day (Fast on 3 Apr 2027; Parana: 4 Apr 2027, 05:20 AM–07:52 AM; Dwadashi ends at 07:56 AM)
Historical Background: Papamochani Ekadashi falls between Holika Dahan and Chaitra Navratri and is the last Ekadashi of the Samvat year. It is is believed to destroy accumulated sins and grant spiritual purification. According to the Papamochani Ekadashi Vrat Katha, Lord Krishna narrated its significance to Arjuna. It is also associated with the story of Medhavi Rishi and Apsara Manjughosa, illustrating the power of repentance and devotion.
Rituals: Nirjala or Phalahar fasting, Sankalpa, worship of Lord Vishnu, chanting Vishnu Sahasranama, recitation of Papamochani Ekadashi Vrat Katha, offering flowers and Tulsi, Aarti, Havan, Bhajans, night vigil (Jagran), charity, and Parana after sunrise on Dwadashi. Devotees abstain from grains and avoid prohibited foods and activities during Dashami, Ekadashi, and Dwadashi.
Fair Activities: Temple worship, bhajans, kirtans, Vrat Katha recitation, Havan, devotional gatherings, charity (daan), spiritual discourses, and distribution of prasadam.
Cultural Significance: Symbolizes repentance, purification, forgiveness, and liberation from sins. Observing this Ekadashi is believed to grant inner peace, religious merit (Punya), and ultimately Moksha (liberation).

Deity: Lord Rama (7th incarnation of Lord Vishnu)
Historical Background: Rama Navami celebrates the birth of Lord Rama, the seventh incarnation of Lord Vishnu, born in Ayodhya to uphold Dharma. His birth is believed to have occurred during Madhyahna, making midday the most auspicious time for worship. The festival is especially significant in Ayodhya, where thousands of devotees gather for grand celebrations.
Rituals: Eight Prahar fasting, Rama Puja during Madhyahna, Ramayana recitation, chanting "Shri Ram", bhajans, temple visits, holy bath in the Sarayu River, processions, charity, and devotional singing.
Fair Activities: Rath Yatras, Ramayana recitations, bhajans, devotional processions, cultural performances, temple fairs, and community feasts.
Cultural Significance: Commemorates the birth of Lord Rama and promotes righteousness (Dharma), truth, devotion, and ideal leadership.

Duration: 1 Day (Fast on 17 Apr 2027; Parana: 18 Apr 2027, 05:01 AM–07:39 AM; Dwadashi ends at 11:12 AM)
Historical Background: Kamada Ekadashi is observed during the Shukla Paksha of Chaitra and is believed to fulfill desires and remove sins. According to the Kamada Ekadashi Vrat Katha, Lord Krishna narrated its importance to Yudhishthira. The story of Lalit and Lalita tells how Lalita observed this fast to free her husband from a curse and restore him to his original Gandharva form.
Rituals: Nirjala or Phalahar fasting, Sankalpa, Vishnu Puja, Vishnu Sahasranama recitation, reading Kamada Ekadashi Vrat Katha, bhajans, Jagran, charity, Tulsi worship, and Parana after sunrise on Dwadashi.
Fair Activities: Temple worship, bhajans, kirtans, Vrat Katha recitation, devotional gatherings, charity (daan), spiritual discourses, and distribution of prasadam.
Cultural Significance: Symbolizes fulfillment of righteous desires, purification, devotion, and liberation from sins. The observance is believed to bring happiness, prosperity, and spiritual upliftment.

Hindu Month: Ashadha (Krishna Paksha) – North India / Jyeshtha (Krishna Paksha) – South India
Historical Background: Yogini Ekadashi is one of the twenty-four Ekadashis dedicated to Lord Vishnu. According to the Padma Purana, observing this fast removes sins and grants spiritual purification. It is associated with the story of King Kubera and his Yaksha servant Hemamali, who was freed from a curse after observing the fast.
Rituals: Observe a day-long fast, worship Lord Vishnu, chant Vishnu Sahasranama, read or listen to the Yogini Ekadashi Vrat Katha, perform bhajans and meditation, and break the fast (Parana) on Dwadashi after Hari Vasara.
Fair Activities: Temple prayers, bhajans, Vishnu Sahasranama recitation, religious discourses (Katha), and community worship; generally no large public fair.
Cultural Significance: Symbolizes repentance, devotion, self-discipline, and spiritual purification. It is believed to remove sins, bring prosperity, and help devotees attain Moksha and Swarga Lok.

Historical Background: Devshayani Ekadashi is observed on the Shukla Paksha Ekadashi of Ashadha. It marks the day when Lord Vishnu enters Yoga Nidra (divine sleep) for four months and awakens on Prabodhini Ekadashi. The festival also marks the beginning of Chaturmas and is associated with the legend of King Mandhata, whose kingdom was freed from famine after observing this Ekadashi.
Rituals: Devotees observe a strict fast, worship Lord Vishnu, offer Tulsi leaves and flowers, chant Vishnu Sahasranama, read the Devshayani Ekadashi Vrat Katha, perform bhajans and kirtans, visit Vishnu temples, and break the fast (Parana) on Dwadashi after sunrise.
Fair Activities: Temple worship, bhajans, kirtans, recitation of Vishnu Sahasranama, religious discourses, and community prayers. In some regions, devotees also participate in Jagannath Rath Yatra celebrations.
Cultural Significance: Devshayani Ekadashi signifies the beginning of Chaturmas and Lord Vishnu's divine sleep. It emphasizes devotion, self-discipline, spiritual purification, and the pursuit of Moksha. Observing the fast is believed to remove sins and bring prosperity and divine blessings.

Region: Maharashtra (also observed in other parts of India)
Duration: 1 Day (In some regions observed from Ashadha Purnima to Shravan Purnima)
Historical Background: Kokila Vrat is dedicated to Goddess Sati and Lord Shiva. According to legend, after Goddess Sati immolated herself when her father insulted Lord Shiva, she lived as a cuckoo (Kokila) for one thousand celestial years before reuniting with Lord Shiva. The vrat is especially observed during years having Adhik Ashadha, though many regions observe it every Ashadha Purnima.
Rituals: Women wake up early, bathe in a river or water body, make a clay idol of a cuckoo, worship Goddess Sati and Lord Shiva, perform Pradosh Puja, observe fasting, listen to the Kokila Vrat Katha, and pray for marital happiness and longevity of their husbands.
Fair Activities: Temple worship, Vrat Katha recitation, women's devotional gatherings, bhajans, and Pradosh Puja. Large public fairs are generally not associated with this vrat.
Cultural Significance: Kokila Vrat symbolizes devotion, marital harmony, fidelity, and the blessings of Goddess Sati. It is believed to grant Akhand Saubhagyavati (eternal marital bliss), protect against widowhood, and bless women with a loving and caring husband.

Historical Background: Vyasa Puja commemorates the birth anniversary of Maharshi Krishnadvaipayana Veda Vyasa, the compiler of the Vedas and author of the Mahabharata. The day is dedicated to Guru worship and celebrates the Guru–Shishya tradition.
Rituals: Devotees perform Guru Puja, worship Veda Vyasa on the Vyasa Peetha, recite the Sankalpa, invoke Brahman, Brahma, Vyasa, Shukadeva, Gaudapada, Govindaswami, and Shankaracharya, offer Akshata, flowers, sandalwood paste, lamps, and seek blessings from their Guru, parents, and elders.
Fair Activities: Guru worship ceremonies, Vedic chanting, scripture recitation, spiritual discourses, satsangs, bhajans, and temple or ashram gatherings.
Cultural Significance: Vyasa Puja honors Maharshi Veda Vyasa and emphasizes the Guru–Shishya tradition, respect for teachers, preservation of sacred knowledge, and the importance of spiritual wisdom in Hindu culture.

Historical Background: Kamika Ekadashi is observed during the Krishna Paksha of Shravana month and is dedicated to Lord Vishnu. According to the Padma Purana, Lord Brahma narrated the greatness of this Ekadashi to Devarshi Narada. It is considered highly sacred for the destruction of sins and attainment of Lord Vishnu's blessings.
Rituals: Devotees observe a strict fast, worship Lord Vishnu, offer Tulsi leaves, chant Vishnu Sahasranama, read the Kamika Ekadashi Vrat Katha, meditate, perform bhajans, stay awake in devotion, and break the fast on Dwadashi during the prescribed Parana time.
Fair Activities: Temple worship, bhajans, Vishnu Sahasranama recitation, Vrat Katha recitation, religious discourses, and community prayers.
Cultural Significance: Kamika Ekadashi is believed to destroy accumulated sins, grant prosperity, increase devotion to Lord Vishnu, and help devotees attain Moksha. Offering Tulsi to Lord Vishnu on this day is considered especially meritorious.

Historical Background: The month of Shravana is dedicated to Lord Shiva. Mondays during this month are considered highly auspicious for Shiva worship. Devotees observe Shravan Somwar Vrat to seek blessings for health, prosperity, marriage, and spiritual progress. Calendar dates vary between Amanta and Purnimanta traditions followed in different regions of India.
Rituals: Devotees fast from sunrise to sunset, perform Rudrabhishek, bathe the Shiva Linga with water, milk, honey and Panchamrit, offer Bilva leaves, Datura flowers, chant "Om Namah Shivaya", visit Shiva temples, and read the Shravan Somwar Vrat Katha.
Fair Activities: Temple visits, Rudrabhishek, Kanwar Yatra in some regions, bhajans, kirtans, community prayers, and religious discourses.
Cultural Significance: Shravan Somwar strengthens devotion to Lord Shiva and is believed to fulfill wishes, remove obstacles, grant marital harmony, good health, prosperity, and spiritual growth.

Region: Maharashtra (also observed in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka and other parts of India)
Historical Background: Mangala Gauri Vrat is observed on every Tuesday of Shravana month by married women, especially newly married women, to seek the blessings of Goddess Gauri for a happy married life, prosperity, and the long life of their husbands. It is one of the most important women's vrats in Maharashtra.
Rituals: Women observe a fast, worship Goddess Gauri, decorate the idol with flowers and ornaments, perform Aarti, offer Naivedya, recite the Mangala Gauri Vrat Katha, sing devotional songs, and pray for Akhand Saubhagya.
Fair Activities: Group worship by women, traditional games, devotional singing, Aarti, temple visits, and cultural gatherings.
Cultural Significance: Mangala Gauri Vrat symbolizes marital harmony, family prosperity, fertility, and devotion to Goddess Gauri. It is believed to bless women with Akhand Saubhagya and family well-being.

Deity: Nag Devta (Ananta, Vasuki, Shesha, Padma, Kambala, Karkotaka, Ashvatara, Dhritarashtra, Shankhapala, Kaliya, Takshaka, Pingala)
Historical Background: Nag Panchami is celebrated on Shukla Paksha Panchami of Shravana and is dedicated to the worship of serpent deities. According to the Vrat Katha, King Janamejaya's Sarpa Yajna was stopped by Astika Muni, saving the serpent race. Snakes are revered as protectors of nature, fertility, and prosperity in Hindu tradition.
Rituals: Devotees worship Nag Devtas at temples, anthills, and snake images, offer milk, flowers, turmeric, sandalwood paste, and sweets, observe fasting, recite Nag Panchami Vrat Katha and mantras, and pray for protection from snake bites and family well-being.
Fair Activities: Worship at serpent temples, community prayers, Nag Panchami fairs, Vrat Katha recitation, devotional singing, and cultural gatherings.
Cultural Significance: Nag Panchami symbolizes reverence for nature and serpent deities, seeking protection, prosperity, fertility, harmony with nature, and family welfare. Worshipping the twelve Nag Devtas is believed to remove fear, evil influences, and snake-related dangers.

Region: Maharashtra (also observed throughout India; especially by the Vaishnava community)
Historical Background: Shravana Putrada Ekadashi is one of the two annual Putrada Ekadashis, the other occurring during Paush Shukla Paksha. It is primarily observed during Shravana Shukla Paksha and is especially important among Vaishnava devotees, where it is also known as Pavitropana Ekadashi or Pavitra Ekadashi. According to the Vrat Katha, the childless King Mahajit was blessed with a son after observing this sacred fast. Traditionally, the vrat is observed by couples praying for virtuous children and family prosperity.
Rituals: Devotees observe a complete or partial fast, worship Lord Vishnu with Tulsi leaves, chant Vishnu Sahasranama, read the Putrada Ekadashi Vrat Katha, perform bhajans, meditate, visit Vishnu temples, remain devoted throughout the day, and break the fast on Dwadashi during the prescribed Parana time.
Fair Activities: Vishnu temple visits, devotional singing, Vishnu Sahasranama recitation, Vrat Katha reading, satsang, community prayers, and religious discourses.
Cultural Significance: The vrat is believed to bless childless couples with virtuous offspring, ensure family prosperity, remove sins, strengthen devotion to Lord Vishnu, and help devotees attain spiritual merit and ultimately Moksha. It also emphasizes the importance of righteous descendants for performing ancestral rites (Shraddha) in Hindu tradition.

Region: Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu
Historical Background: Varalakshmi Vratam is observed on the last Friday of Shravana Shukla Paksha in honour of Goddess Varalakshmi, a benevolent form of Mahalakshmi who emerged from the Kshir Sagar (Ocean of Milk). According to tradition, worshipping Varalakshmi grants prosperity, health, children, wealth and all auspicious blessings. It is one of the most important festivals for married women in South India and Maharashtra.
Rituals: Married women observe a fast, install a Kalash symbolizing Goddess Lakshmi, decorate it with saree and ornaments, perform Lakshmi Puja, chant Lakshmi mantras, tie the sacred Dorak thread, offer Vayana (traditional sweets), perform Aarti and pray for the well-being of their family.
Fair Activities: Lakshmi Puja, bhajans, devotional singing, women's group worship, temple visits, cultural gatherings and religious discourses.
Cultural Significance: The festival symbolizes prosperity, family welfare, marital happiness and abundance. Worship of Varalakshmi is believed to bestow the blessings of Ashtalakshmi (the eight forms of Goddess Lakshmi) and ensure lasting wealth and good fortune.

Region: Maharashtra (also celebrated across India, especially South India)
Historical Background: Gayatri Jayanti commemorates the birth of Goddess Gayatri, revered as Veda Mata (Mother of the Vedas). She is regarded as the embodiment of divine wisdom and is identified with Saraswati, Lakshmi and Parvati. The day is also observed as Sanskrit Diwas in modern India to promote the Sanskrit language and Vedic heritage.
Rituals: Devotees worship Goddess Gayatri, chant the Gayatri Mantra repeatedly, perform Havan (Yajna), meditate, read sacred scriptures, visit temples and participate in spiritual discourses.
Fair Activities: Gayatri Havan, Vedic chanting, Sanskrit seminars, religious discourses, temple worship, cultural programs and community prayers.
Cultural Significance: Gayatri Jayanti promotes spiritual knowledge, wisdom, purity of mind, devotion and preservation of Vedic culture. Observing the festival is believed to bring intellectual growth, inner peace and divine blessings.

Deity: Lord Kalki (10th Avatar of Lord Vishnu)
Historical Background: Kalki Jayanti commemorates the future incarnation of Lord Vishnu as Kalki, the tenth and final avatar who is prophesied to appear at the end of Kali Yuga. According to Hindu scriptures, Lord Kalki will be born as the son of the Brahmin Vishnuyash in the village of Shambhal to destroy evil, restore Dharma and usher in a new Satya Yuga. The festival symbolizes hope for the triumph of righteousness over unrighteousness.
Rituals: Devotees observe fasts, worship Lord Vishnu and Lord Kalki, perform special Puja during the auspicious Muhurat, recite Vishnu Sahasranama, Bhagavad Gita and Kalki-related scriptures, offer prayers in Vishnu temples, perform Aarti and seek blessings for righteousness and spiritual progress.
Fair Activities: Vishnu temple celebrations, devotional singing (Bhajans), religious discourses, scripture recitation, community prayers and cultural programs.
Cultural Significance: Kalki Jayanti reminds devotees that righteousness ultimately triumphs over evil. The festival inspires faith in divine justice, encourages moral living and strengthens devotion to Lord Vishnu while emphasizing the restoration of Dharma.

Region: Madhya Pradesh/ Maharashtra/Mathura/Vrindavan/ and other parts of India
Historical Background: Ranga Panchami is celebrated on the fifth day after Holi and marks the culmination of Holi festivities in many regions. The festival commemorates Lord Krishna playing Holi with Radha Rani using colors and Gulal. It is celebrated with great enthusiasm in Madhya Pradesh, especially Ujjain, as well as in Mathura and Vrindavan where Rangotsava and special temple celebrations are organized.
Rituals: Playing with Gulal and colored powders, Krishna-Radha worship, Rangotsava, temple processions, devotional singing, cultural performances, community gatherings, and special tableaux in temples.
Fair Activities: Color-throwing celebrations, Rangotsava, cultural programs, temple fairs, devotional music, dance performances, and community processions.
Cultural Significance: Celebrates the divine love of Radha and Krishna, symbolizes joy, unity, devotion, and the triumph of happiness over negativity while marking the conclusion of Holi festivities.

Alternate Name: Yugadi/ Telugu New Year/Kannada New Year
Region: Andhra Pradesh/ Telangana/Karnataka (celebrated as Yugadi)/Maharashtra (as Gudi Padwa)
Category: New Year Festival / Cultural & Religious Festival
Deity: Lord Brahma (creator of the universe)/worship of household and village deities
Historical Background: Ugadi marks the beginning of the Hindu Luni-Solar New Year and the start of a new Samvatsara (one of the sixty-year cycle). It is celebrated as the New Year in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, as Yugadi in Karnataka, and on the same day as Gudi Padwa in Maharashtra. According to tradition, Lord Brahma began the creation of the universe on this day. A unique celebration takes place in Medapuram, Sri Sathya Sai district, where the Madiga community carries the deity in a grand procession followed by Panju Seva.
Rituals: Ritual oil bath (Abhyanga Snana), house cleaning and decoration, Rangoli, worship of deities, Panchanga Shravanam (listening to the New Year almanac), eating Ugadi Pachadi (a mixture symbolizing the six tastes of life), Neem leaf consumption, temple visits, processions, Panju Seva, Aarti, and distribution of Prasadam.
Fair Activities: Temple processions, Panchanga reading ceremonies, cultural performances, devotional music, decorated chariots and bullock carts, community feasts, Panju Seva, and Prasadam distribution.
Cultural Significance: Marks the beginning of the Hindu New Year, symbolizes renewal, prosperity, hope, and acceptance of all experiences in life through the six flavors of Ugadi Pachadi. It preserves regional traditions and strengthens community bonds.

Alternate Name: Bhaiya Dooj/ Bhai Phonta/Bhai Tika/ Bhav Bij
Historical Background: According to Hindu mythology, Yamraj visited his sister Yamuna, who welcomed him with tilak and aarti and prayed for his long life. Yamraj declared that brothers receiving tilak from their sisters on this day would have long and healthy lives.
Rituals: Sisters prepare a rice-flour seat; apply vermillion, dahi and rice tika; place Kaddu flower, betel leaves, betel nuts and coins in brother's palms; pour water while chanting mantras; tie Kalawa; perform aarti; exchange gifts; take elders' blessings
Fair Activities: Family/sibling celebrations
Cultural Significance: Reinforces family bonding, love, mutual respect and the brother-sister relationship; brothers vow to protect sisters

Rituals: Abhyanga Snan before sunrise; herbal-oil massage; clean/new clothes; Kula Devi temple visit; lighting diyas; ancestor offerings in some areas; fireworks
Fair Activities: Fireworks; lighting diyas; family and temple visits
Cultural Significance: Symbolizes victory of good/light over evil/darkness, removal of negative energies and a fresh beginning

Region: Maharashtra/less widely observed in North India
Duration: 3 days of rituals; main puja on Friday
Historical Background: Varalakshmi is a form of Goddess Mahalakshmi and the consort of Lord Vishnu. She is believed to have emerged from the milky ocean and to grant boons and fulfil devotees' desires. Worshipping Varalakshmi is believed to be equivalent to worshipping the eight forms of Lakshmi (Ashtalakshmi).
Rituals: Married women primarily observe the fast in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra; early morning head bath; cleaning and decorating house with rangoli; Kalasha preparation; sandalwood paste; Swastika; raw rice, coins, turmeric and leaves in Kalasha; mango leaves and turmeric-smeared coconut; Ganesha worship; slokas; arati; yellow thread tying; gift exchange; Kalasha dismantled after bath
Fair Activities: Home puja; rangoli decoration; gift exchange
Cultural Significance: Brings peace, prosperity, financial blessings and family well-being; prayers for husband, children and family; represents the eight forms of prosperity/Ashtalakshmi

Historical Background: Akshaya Tritiya is considered an auspicious day associated with prosperity, good fortune and activities believed to bring lasting benefits. It is also associated with the birth anniversary of Lord Parashurama.
Rituals: Worship of Vishnu and Lakshmi; prayers; charity; purchasing gold and other auspicious items; beginning new ventures; religious observances
Fair Activities: Religious gatherings; charity; purchase of gold; beginning new ventures
Cultural Significance: Considered an auspicious day for prosperity, charity, new beginnings, marriage and important purchases; the word “Akshaya” signifies something that does not diminish

Category: Traditional Girls’ and Women’s Festival; Folk Songs and Dance
Hindu Month: Bhadrapada Purnima to Ashwin Purnima (Kojagiri Purnima); Ashwin Shukla Paksha Dashami (Dasara) to Purnima
Duration: Traditionally about one month; in some places, from Dasara to Kojagiri Purnima
Historical Background: Bhulabai is identified with Goddess Parvati in Marathi folklore. The festival is associated with Parvati’s married life, motherhood, fertility, and women’s experiences. Traditionally observed for about a month, the celebration was reported to have shortened in some places by 2020. In 2025, a Zilla Parishad school in Buldhana celebrated it so students could continue learning its songs and customs.
Rituals: Installing Bhulabai, Bhuloji and Ganesh idols; gathering in the evening; visiting houses in groups; singing traditional songs; dancing; playing with tipri sticks; performing aarti; guessing the covered khirapat; night vigil on Kojagiri Purnima; immersing idols the following morning
Fair Activities: Folk singing and dancing, Bhondla dance, traditional games, house-to-house visits and identifying the khirapat
Cultural Significance: Reflects women’s social experiences through folk songs and connects the festival with the agricultural season, harvest, community interaction and transmission of traditional songs and customs to younger generations

Historical Background: First day of the Hindu year.
Rituals: Gudhis and toranas are erected and worshipped in front of every house.
Fair Activities: Family celebration
Cultural Significance: Marks the beginning of the Hindu New Year.
